reviewed.student: Why does a ball slow down as it goes up?
reviewed.tutor: Good question. Watch the ball go up. It slows, and stops for an instant at the top. Gravity pulls down the whole time. Which way is the ball moving, and which way is gravity pulling?

reviewed.student: because gravity pulls on it?
reviewed.tutor: Yes, that's the reason. Gravity pulls down, the ball moves up, so the pull works against the motion and eats away its speed. Each second it loses about ten metres per second. Now, what happens to the speed once the ball starts falling?
refused: highlight needs writeMath, but pull is a vector

reviewed.student: so at the very top its speed is zero?
reviewed.tutor: Yes, for that instant. Its upward speed hits zero right there. But gravity is still pulling, so it doesn't stay stopped. It starts falling straight away. Is gravity zero at the top, too?

reviewed.student: wait, then why doesn't it just stay up there?
reviewed.tutor: Great follow-up. Look at the arrow on the ball. Gravity doesn't switch off at the top. Speed is zero for an instant, but the pull is still there. So what do you think a pull downward does to a ball that isn't moving?

reviewed.student: oh ok. how fast does it fall after one second?
reviewed.tutor: Good, let's work it out. Starting from rest, speed equals gravity's pull times time. Gravity adds about nine point eight metres per second every second. So what's the speed after one second?

reviewed.student: and after two seconds?
reviewed.tutor: Try it yourself. Gravity adds nine point eight each second, and you've got two seconds. What do you get for the speed?

reviewed.student: I don't get why it's the same pull all the way
reviewed.tutor: Fair question. Near Earth's surface, gravity's pull on the ball is basically constant. Going a few metres up barely changes your distance from Earth's centre, which is thousands of kilometres. So the pull hardly changes. Does that make sense so far?

reviewed.student: can you show me on the board?
reviewed.tutor: Sure. Here's the idea in words, since I can't draw the planet. The ball climbs maybe three metres, against six thousand four hundred kilometres to Earth's centre. That's a change of about one part in two million. Why would the pull barely notice that?

reviewed.student: what if I throw it harder?
reviewed.tutor: Good one. Watch. It goes much higher, but gravity still takes the same ten metres per second each second. So it just takes longer to use up the speed. How many seconds do you think it needs?

reviewed.student: does it go twice as high if I throw twice as fast?
reviewed.tutor: Nice guess, but no. Think about time first. Twice the speed means twice the time to stop, and the average speed is also twice as big. So the height is multiplied by two times two. How many times higher is that?
